rows.one_line_why: Cites the BLS Employment Situation report for Dec 2021 but does not state the actual figure.
Official BLS data shows manufacturing employment at 12.559M in Jan 2022 vs 12.190M in Dec 2020, a gain of 369,000—exactly matching the claim.
References BLS CES highlights for Dec 2021 over-the-year gains but does not state the specific figure.
BLS Monthly Labor Review states manufacturing employment grew by 365,000 in 2021, contradicting the claim of 369,000.
Indicates the BLS CES series is available for computation but does not itself state the figure.
Provides a pre-benchmark manufacturing level but does not state the year-over-year or calendar-year change.
Primary FRED/BLS data series MANEMP shows Dec 2020 at 12,190 thousand and Dec 2021 at 12,546 thousand, a gain of 356,000—not 369,000.
BLS CES highlights state 12.559M in Jan 2022 and 12.190M in Dec 2020, implying a gain of 369,000, matching the claim.
JEC fact sheet asserts manufacturing job gains in 2021 but does not state the specific 369,000 figure.
JEC fact sheet on manufacturing progress is cited as source of the talking point but the snippet does not state the actual figure.
Claim asserts >$1T deficit cut in a single year; snippet shows FY2021 deficit fell only $360B (from $3.1T to $2.8T), far below $1T threshold.

OMB Historical Table 1.1 shows no prior single-year deficit decline exceeding $1T through its coverage, supporting the 'only president ever' superlative but contradicting that the claim's subject achieved it.
Source identifies the data series needed to test the claim but does not itself present figures or comparisons.
CBO Monthly Budget Review for Feb 2022 provides running FY2022 data but snippet does not state actual year-over-year deficit change.
CBO Historical Budget Data (1962–present) shows no prior >$1T single-year deficit drops in recent history, consistent with 'only president ever' but does not confirm the claim's subject achieved it.
Source identifies the official baseline but does not present the deficit figures or year-over-year changes needed to evaluate the claim.

FRED FYFSD series (OMB source) shows FY2020 deficit of −3,131,917M and FY2021 deficit of −2,772,179M; year-over-year improvement is 359,738M (~$360B), not >$1T; no prior year shows >$1T single-year deficit reduction.
CBO infographic provides context on FY2021 deficit level but does not present the year-over-year change or historical comparisons needed to test the claim.
CRFB analysis discusses whether Biden's $1T claim and FY2022 movements would make him unique, but snippet does not state the actual deficit figures or conclusion.
Confirms FY2021 deficit of $2.8T and $360B reduction from 2020, explicitly framing whether a >$1T single-year cut was realized or merely projected—the realized cut fell far short.
Claim asserts economy is growing; BEA official data shows 3.5% real GDP growth for 2005, supporting growth assertion, though Q4 slowdown to 1.1% raises questions about 'vigorous'.
Employment Situation report cited but snippet does not provide the actual payroll or unemployment figures needed to assess health claim.
Official BEA data: 3.5% real GDP growth for 2005 directly supports the 'growing' assertion in the claim.
OECD Economic Outlook tables show U.S. real GDP growth above Euro area and Japan, directly supporting claim that U.S. is growing faster than other major industrialized nations.
BLS payroll summary cited but snippet does not provide the actual multi-year job change figures needed to assess the health claim.
BLS December 2005 unemployment at 4.9% with continued payroll gains supports the 'healthy' labor market assertion.
IMF statement that U.S. continued to lead global recovery and outpace most trading partners directly supports claim of faster growth than other major industrialized nations.
FRED PAYEMS series shows nonfarm payrolls rose from 130,255K (Dec 2003) to 134,468K (Dec 2005), a gain of 4,213K jobs over 24 months, supporting 'healthy' economy assertion.
Official BEA advance release confirms 3.5% real GDP growth for 2005, supporting the 'growing' assertion.
Congressional JEC notes Q4 2005 GDP growth of 1.1% fell well below 3.0% consensus, contradicting the 'vigorous' characterization of growth.
CRS table shows 1981 minimum $3.35 = $8.61 in real (2013) dollars; $7.25 in 2014 is ~16% below $8.61, not ~20%.
EPI explicitly calculates 1981 minimum as $8.24 in 2013 dollars versus $7.25 current, yielding ~12% decline, contradicting the ~20% claim.
Notes erosion of purchasing power but provides no specific percentage figure to compare against the 20% claim.
BLS CPI-U series is a component needed for inflation adjustment but does not itself state the minimum-wage comparison or the 20% figure.
Identifies nominal wage history ($3.35 in 1981, $7.25 in 2014) but does not perform or state the real-value comparison.
References a real minimum-wage series in 2013 dollars showing decline since early 1980s but snippet does not quote the specific percentage.
Contextual White House framing document; does not contain the quantitative comparison at issue.
Addresses minimum wage as share of median wage, not real purchasing power decline since Reagan era.
Primary BLS Employment Situation report for January 2026 is the official source needed to verify the record-high claim, but snippet does not state the actual figure.
BLS time-series CE16OV shows January 2026 employed persons at 164,520K, which is higher than the prior all-time high of 163,992K in December 2025, supporting the claim.
Official BLS Employment Situation for January 2026 is the authoritative source but snippet does not provide the specific employment level figure.
FRED CE16OV series shows January 2026 employed persons at 164,520K, exceeding the prior record of 163,992K in December 2025, confirming the claim.
Archived BLS release for January 2026 is the primary source but snippet does not state the actual employment figures.
States all-time high was 163,992K in December 2025 with January/February 2026 revisions showing declines, contradicting the claim that more Americans are working today.

PAYEMS nonfarm payroll series (establishment survey) is a different employment measure than household-survey employed persons; January 2026 shows 158,627K but this is not the series the claim rests on.
Reference to LNS12000000 series is relevant but snippet provides no actual figures for comparison.
News coverage of January 2026 jobs report is background context but does not provide the specific employment level needed to verify the record-high assertion.
Cites BLS data showing all-time high of 163,992K in December 2025; claim asserts more Americans working today, and January 2026 CE16OV data (164,520K) confirms this exceeds that prior peak.
BLS official series shows peak of $6.227/doz (Mar 2025) to $2.577/doz (Jan 2026), a decline of 58.6%, which rounds to the claimed 60%.
Source explicitly states Mar 2025 peak $6.227/doz and Jan 2026 $2.577/doz represent 'about a 59–60% decline,' directly corroborating the claim.
USDA ERS documents the same retail peak ($6.23/doz in Mar 2025) and subsequent sharp declines into 2026, consistent with the 60% drop claim.
Published report from Feb 13, 2026 states retail eggs down 34% year-over-year, contradicting the 60% claim (though YoY and peak-to-current are different baselines).
Confirms general downward trend in retail egg prices but provides no specific quantitative figure to compare against the 60% claim.
Describes prices as 'markedly lower' by late Feb 2026 but does not provide the specific percentage decline needed to verify the 60% figure.
Reports cage-free egg prices showing declines in early 2026 but does not quantify the magnitude relative to the 60% claim.
References 'scale of the early-2026 egg price decline' but provides no specific percentage or numerical comparison.
Notes that 'magnitude of decline depends on baseline' but does not itself provide figures or resolve which baseline applies to the 60% claim.
Lists advertised retail prices supporting lower consumer prices in early 2026 but does not quantify the percentage decline.
Claim asserts prices are lower; BLS data shows rent +5.1% YoY, lodging -3.0%, used cars -1.8%, new vehicles +0.1%—most items up, contradicting 'lower by a lot'.
BLS January 2026 CPI tables show food, shelter and indexed items flat or higher versus Jan 2025, directly contradicting the claim of prices lower by a lot.
Provides baseline CPI data from January 2025 (likely office-taking date) but does not itself compare to January 2026 or state whether prices rose or fell.
Full BLS January 2026 CPI release with category detail tables is a primary source document but snippet does not state the actual price direction or magnitudes.
Confirms the claim was made on Feb 24, 2026, but does not address whether prices are actually lower or higher.
January 2026 CPI report states shelter and food categories still rising over the year, contradicting the claim that these items are lower.
Promises detailed category breakdown for chicken, butter, fruit, rent but snippet itself does not provide the actual figures or direction.
NBC grocery tracker shows chicken and butter rose since Trump took office January 2025; only eggs were an exception, contradicting claim of lower prices.
FRED primary CPI series for poultry (CUUR0000SAF112) shows 339.169 in Jan 2025 and 346.613 in Jan 2026, a +2.2% increase, contradicting claim of lower prices.
